about: Plain explanations of mining words used in the colliery histories. Each entry: term, other forms that should link to it, and the explanation. Edit freely.

terms.text: Hard coal. It burns hot and clean with little smoke, and nearly all of America's anthracite lies in four fields in northeastern Pennsylvania.
A coal mine together with everything on the surface that served it: the breaker, engine houses, shops, stables and railroad sidings.
The tall building where coal from the mine was crushed, sorted into sizes and cleaned of slate and rock before it was loaded into railroad cars.
A boy, often 8 to 14 years old, who sat over the coal chutes in a breaker picking out slate and rock by hand.
Another name for a breaker boy, or an old miner no longer fit for underground work, picking slate out of the coal in the breaker.
A plant that recovered small coal from old refuse banks by washing and screening it.
Waste from the breaker: small coal, slate and rock too poor to sell when it was dumped.
A hill of breaker waste piled beside a colliery. Many are still there, and some were later reworked for the coal left in them.
A layer of coal in the ground. Anthracite veins have names like Mammoth, Buck Mountain, Skidmore and Primrose, and each colliery worked several.
The thickest and most valuable anthracite vein, in places 20 to 60 feet thick.
A vertical opening from the surface down to the coal, with a cage that raised and lowered men and cars.
An opening driven down at an angle, following a vein, with cars hauled up and down it on a rope.
A level opening driven straight into a hillside where a vein reaches the surface.
A level passage driven through rock to reach a vein, or to connect one vein to another.
The main underground haulage road along a vein, with track for mine cars. Breasts were worked upward from it.
A room cut upward from the gangway where a miner and his laborer dug the coal.
A block of coal left standing between breasts to hold up the roof.
Taking out the coal pillars at the end of a mine's life. It recovered more coal but was among the most dangerous work, since the roof could fall at any time.
One level of a slope or shaft. When the coal above was worked out, the slope was sunk another lift deeper.
A steep track up a hillside, with cars pulled up by a rope and engine, used to bring coal to the breaker or carry refuse to the bank.
The tall frame over a shaft holding the wheels the hoisting ropes run over.
A big ventilating fan that pushed or pulled fresh air through the mine to carry gas away.
Methane gas given off by coal. Mixed with air it explodes when it meets a flame.
The poisonous gases left after an explosion. It often killed more men than the blast itself.
The man who went through the mine before each shift testing for gas, and marked places unsafe to enter.
The skilled man who cut and blasted the coal in a breast. He was paid by the car and hired his own laborer.
The man who loaded the coal the miner blasted down. Many laborers later became miners themselves.
A boy who opened and closed the ventilation doors underground so cars could pass while the air kept flowing where it should.
The boy or man who drove the mules that pulled mine cars along the gangways.
A worker who slowed runaway cars by jamming wooden sprags into their wheels.
A slow-burning fuse used to set off a blast. A squib that seemed to have gone out could still fire, which killed many men.
A sudden slide of loose coal down a breast or chute, which could bury a man.
A sloping trough that carried coal down from a breast to the cars in the gangway.
A small village of company houses built beside a colliery for its workers' families.
Mining from the surface by stripping off the rock above the coal with big shovels and draglines.
Coal from the lower veins that leaves a reddish ash when burned.
A breaker machine that separated coal from slate by pulsing water: the heavier slate sank and the coal stayed on top.
